questions.stem: A person owns a house alone, with no co-owner. That form of ownership is called:
questions.explanation: Severalty means the estate is severed from everyone else: one owner. Joint tenancy and tenancy in common require more than one owner.

questions.stem: Two friends buy a duplex. The deed says they may have unequal shares and that a deceased owner's share passes by will, not automatically to the survivor. They most likely hold title as:
choices: Joint tenants with right of survivorship
questions.explanation: Tenants in common may hold unequal shares, and there is no right of survivorship. A joint tenancy's signature feature is survivorship.

questions.stem: Four unities — time, title, interest, and possession — are associated with which ownership form?
questions.explanation: Traditional joint tenancy is created when the co-owners take the same interest, at the same time, by the same instrument, with equal rights of possession. Tenancy in common requires only unity of possession.

questions.stem: A joint tenant sells that tenant's share to a new buyer. As to the remaining original joint tenant and the buyer, the ownership typically becomes:
questions.explanation: Conveying one joint tenant's interest breaks the unities as to that share. The buyer and the remaining owner hold as tenants in common.

questions.stem: Grandparent deeds a house to a child for the child's life, and then to a grandchild. The grandchild's future interest is a:
questions.explanation: The child has a life estate. The grandchild holds the remainder, which becomes possessory when the life estate ends. A reversion would come back to the original grantor.

questions.stem: A landowner keeps the right to get the property back when a life estate ends. That future interest is a:
questions.explanation: If the grantor does not give the future interest to someone else, it reverts to the grantor, or the grantor's estate, when the measuring life ends.

questions.stem: A fence built by the neighbor crosses two feet onto the owner's lot. The fence is an example of:
questions.explanation: An encroachment is a physical intrusion of a structure or object onto another's land. It can cloud title and affect value even when no easement was granted.

questions.stem: A written right to cross a neighbor's driveway to reach a landlocked back lot, intended to benefit that lot, is typically:
choices: A license that always transfers with the person only
questions.explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits a parcel (the dominant estate) and burdens another (the servient estate). It generally transfers with the land.

questions.stem: A utility company holds a right to run lines across many parcels, and the right does not benefit a neighboring lot the company owns. That right is typically:
questions.explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity rather than a neighboring parcel. Utility rights are the classic example.

questions.stem: Permission to park on a neighbor's field for one weekend, revocable at the neighbor's will, is a:
questions.explanation: A license is permission, not an interest in land. Unlike an easement, it is generally revocable and does not bind later owners by itself.

questions.stem: Mineral rights are sold, but the seller keeps the house and yard. Those minerals are an example of:
choices: Personal property only if still in the ground
A fixture that lost its identity
Rights that can be severed from the surface
questions.explanation: Air, mineral, and water rights may be conveyed separately from the surface. The buyer of the minerals holds an interest in real property.

questions.stem: A freestanding refrigerator in a rented apartment, installed by the tenant and removable without damage, is ordinarily:
choices: A fixture that belongs to the landlord automatically
Real property because it is indoors
questions.explanation: Personal property is movable. An item becomes a fixture, and part of the real estate, when it is annexed with the intent that it stay. A freestanding appliance usually remains personal property.

questions.stem: Which description starts at a monument and follows distances and compass directions around the parcel?
choices: A rectangular government survey township only
questions.explanation: Metes are distances and bounds are directions or boundaries. Lot and block refers to a recorded plat. A street address is not a legal description.

questions.stem: A deed describes the land as 'Lot 12, Block 4, of Shoreline Map, recorded in Map Book 9, page 22.' That is:
choices: A metes-and-bounds call without a plat
questions.explanation: Lot and block, also called a recorded plat, identifies a parcel by lot and block on a map filed in the land records.

questions.stem: In the government rectangular survey, a section contains about how many acres?
questions.explanation: A township is about 36 sections. A standard section is about one square mile, or 640 acres. 43,560 is the number of square feet in one acre.

questions.stem: A town's unpaid property tax is a lien. In general, that lien:
choices: Erases all mortgages automatically on the due date
Is only a personal promise with no effect on title
Encumbers the property and can lead to a tax sale if unpaid
questions.explanation: A property-tax lien attaches to the real estate. It can affect title and value and, if enforced, can result in a tax foreclosure or sale. Priority rules vary, but the lien is real.

questions.stem: A contractor who supplied labor for a kitchen and was not paid may look to:
choices: A mechanic's lien, if the statutory steps are followed
questions.explanation: Mechanic's lien statutes let unpaid contractors and suppliers claim a lien against the improved property when they follow the required notices and deadlines.

questions.stem: A buyer at a closing discovers the seller's cousin has an unreleased mortgage on the property. That mortgage is:
choices: A lien that can prevent marketable title until it is released or paid
questions.explanation: A mortgage is a lien. An unreleased lien is an encumbrance. Buyers and title insurers treat open liens as title problems.

questions.stem: Which interest is measured by someone's lifetime and then ends?
choices: An estate for years of five calendar years
questions.explanation: A life estate lasts for the measuring life and then passes as a remainder or reversion. A fee simple can last forever. An estate for years is a lease for a fixed term.

questions.stem: A cooperative buyer generally receives:
choices: A fee-simple deed to the airspace only
Shares in a corporation and a proprietary lease, rather than a deed to a unit
An easement in gross and nothing else
questions.explanation: In a co-op, the corporation owns the real estate. The resident owns stock and the right to occupy under a proprietary lease. A condominium owner, by contrast, holds title to a unit.

questions.stem: In a condominium, the owner typically holds title to a unit plus:
choices: No interest in hallways or grounds
Sole ownership of the exterior roof in severalty
An undivided interest in the common elements
questions.explanation: Condominium ownership combines a separate unit interest with a shared interest in common elements such as halls, grounds, and the structure, subject to the declaration and bylaws.

questions.stem: A time-share purchaser most nearly has:
choices: A fee simple in the entire building all year
Only a personal license that can never be recorded
A right to use, or an interval ownership in, property for recurring periods
questions.explanation: Time-shares divide use or ownership into intervals. The form can be a deeded interest or a right-to-use contract. It is a common-interest arrangement the exam outline treats separately from a full-year fee simple.

questions.stem: Land is described as the north half of the northeast quarter of a section. About how many acres is that?
questions.explanation: A section is about 640 acres. A quarter section is about 160. Half of that quarter is about 80 acres.

questions.stem: Water rights that go with land touching a river are generally called:
choices: Littoral rights, which is the term for ocean or lake frontage only in some texts, but not for a river
questions.explanation: Riparian rights concern land bordering flowing water such as a river or stream. Littoral rights concern land bordering a lake, sea, or similar body. The labels are the ones the exam expects.

questions.stem: Crops already planted by a tenant, which the tenant has the right to harvest, are called:
questions.explanation: Emblements are annual crops produced by labor. A tenant who planted them may usually return to harvest them even after the tenancy ends. They are treated as personal property.

questions.stem: A bookstore tenant bolts custom shelves to the walls. The shelves were installed for the business and can be removed, repairing the wall. They are:
choices: Real property the moment they are bolted
questions.explanation: Trade fixtures are personal property of the commercial tenant, installed for business, and removable before the lease ends if the premises are restored.

questions.stem: Which item is real property?
choices: A freestanding washer with a plug
A built-in dishwasher wired and plumbed into the kitchen
A framed poster leaning on a shelf
questions.explanation: Annexation, adaptation, and the intent to make the item a permanent part of the building point to a fixture. Built-in, plumbed appliances are usually fixtures. Freestanding items usually are not.

questions.stem: Adverse possession is a way a person may gain title by possessing land in a way that is open and hostile for the statutory period. It is best classified as:
choices: A potential encumbrance or threat to the record owner's title while the period runs, and a title claim if it ripens
questions.explanation: The outline treats adverse possession as a potential encumbrance on title. If the possession meets the state's tests for the required years, the possessor may gain title. Permission from the owner defeats hostility.

questions.stem: The government's power to take private land for public use, with just compensation, is:
questions.explanation: Eminent domain is the taking power. The court process is condemnation. Police power regulates without a taking. Escheat sends ownerless property to the state.

questions.stem: Property taxes and special assessments exist because government has the power of:
questions.explanation: Taxation is an independent governmental power. A special assessment is a charge for a local improvement, such as a sidewalk, that benefits particular parcels.

questions.stem: When a person dies with no will and no heirs who can take the land, title may pass to the state by:
questions.explanation: Escheat is the fallback when ownership has nowhere else to go. It is not a taking for a highway, and it is not a zoning relief valve.

questions.stem: A zoning board allows a homeowner to build closer to the lot line than the ordinance permits, because strict enforcement would cause undue hardship. That relief is a:
questions.explanation: A variance is permission to vary from the zoning rules for a specific parcel, usually after a hardship showing. A nonconforming use is a use that was legal before the rule changed.

questions.stem: A warehouse legally operated before the area was rezoned residential. It may usually continue as:
choices: A variance that must be reapplied for every week
questions.explanation: Nonconforming uses are grandfathered. They can often continue, but expansion or reconstruction after destruction may be limited by the ordinance.

questions.stem: Deed restrictions and subdivision covenants are examples of:
questions.explanation: Private controls come from owners and developers: conditions, covenants, and restrictions. Zoning, building codes, and eminent domain are public controls.

questions.stem: A subdivision's CC&Rs ban overnight boat parking. Those rules are enforced by:
choices: The owners, often through the association, as private covenants
A title insurance company as a tax collector
questions.explanation: Covenants, conditions, and restrictions run with the land when properly created. Neighbors or the association enforce them. They are not the same tool as a tax lien.

questions.stem: Building codes mainly regulate:
choices: How structures are designed and built, for safety
The interest rate on a mortgage
questions.explanation: Building codes set construction standards. Zoning regulates use and bulk. They work together but they are not the same ordinance.

questions.stem: Flood-zone rules and inland-wetland rules are examples of:
choices: Government controls on special land types
questions.explanation: The outline groups flood zones and wetlands as regulation of special land. Development there can require extra permits, elevation, or setbacks.

questions.stem: A buyer plans a daycare in a house zoned single-family only. The licensee should:
choices: Tell the buyer to verify zoning and any needed approvals before relying on that use
Record a new deed that changes the zone
Ignore use and discuss only paint colors
Promise the use is legal because the house has a kitchen
questions.explanation: A licensee does not rezone property by optimism. Proposed use is a reason to check public and private land-use controls before the buyer is locked in.

questions.stem: Lead, asbestos, underground tanks, and mold are grouped on the outline as:
choices: Environmental hazards that can affect use, value, and disclosure
questions.explanation: Environmental hazards can limit use, require abatement, and be material facts. The exam expects you to recognize the hazard, not to design the cleanup.

questions.stem: A contaminated site with a recorded restriction on future use is an example of:
choices: A fee simple that cannot be limited
A land-use control tied to environmental condition
questions.explanation: Agencies can require institutional controls, such as deed notices or use limits, so later owners do not treat a cleaned-up or contained site as unrestricted.

questions.stem: Police power, in land-use terms, is the power to:
choices: Regulate for health, safety, and general welfare, such as through zoning
Set the broker's commission by statute in every town
Take land for a highway without paying
questions.explanation: Zoning and building codes are exercises of police power. Eminent domain requires compensation. Commission rates are not set by the police power.

questions.stem: A homeowner asks the city to allow a small café in a residential zone because the plan meets special criteria in the ordinance. That approval, if granted, is most like:
choices: A special permit or conditional use
questions.explanation: Conditional or special-use permits allow a use the ordinance contemplates, if conditions are met. A variance relaxes a dimensional or similar rule because of hardship.

questions.stem: Private restrictions and zoning both limit a lot. When they differ, the owner must generally follow:
choices: Only zoning, because deeds cannot restrict use
Only the private rule, because zoning never applies
questions.explanation: Both can apply at once. The owner does not get to pick the looser one. A deed covenant can be tighter than zoning, and zoning can forbid something the deed allows.

questions.stem: A special assessment for a new sidewalk is typically charged:
choices: As a federal income tax on the licensee
Only to tenants in a month-to-month lease
To the owners who benefit from that improvement
As a transfer tax on every deed in the state
questions.explanation: Special assessments fund local improvements and are allocated to benefited parcels. They are not the same as the conveyance tax on a deed.

questions.stem: An appraiser estimates value for a lender's loan. A salesperson's price opinion for a listing is:
choices: A certified appraisal if the salesperson is careful
The definition of market value in every case
A comparative market analysis, which is not an appraisal
questions.explanation: A CMA or BPO helps a client pick a price. Calling it an appraisal, or performing appraisal work that requires a license, is unauthorized appraisal practice.

questions.stem: The sales-comparison approach relies mainly on:
choices: The cost to rebuild minus depreciation only
Net operating income divided by a cap rate only
Recent prices of similar properties, adjusted for differences
questions.explanation: Buyers and appraisers compare the subject to sold comps and adjust for differences such as size, condition, and location. That is the approach most used for houses.

questions.stem: A brand-new house with no useful sales nearby is often best supported by:
choices: A gross-rent multiplier taken from a distant factory
The income approach using zero rent
questions.explanation: The cost approach estimates land value plus the cost of a new building, minus depreciation. It fits new or special-purpose property when comps are thin.

questions.stem: Reproduction cost means the cost to:
choices: Build a similar utility with modern materials
Build an exact replica, using the same materials and design
questions.explanation: Reproduction copies the original. Replacement builds something with similar usefulness using current methods. The exam uses those words differently.

questions.stem: An apartment building is valued mainly by:
choices: The color of the lobby only
questions.explanation: Income property is bought for its net income. Value can be estimated by capitalizing net operating income or by using a gross-rent multiplier.

questions.stem: Net operating income divided by a capitalization rate produces an estimate of:
questions.explanation: The income formula is value = NOI / cap rate. Rearranged, cap rate = NOI / value, and NOI = value × cap rate.

questions.stem: Which expense is subtracted to reach net operating income?
choices: Depreciation taken on the tax return
Ordinary operating expenses such as insurance, taxes, and maintenance
questions.explanation: NOI is income after operating expenses and before debt service and income taxes. Mortgage payments are not an operating expense in the cap-rate formula.

questions.stem: A comp sold for $20,000 more because it has a garage the subject lacks. In the sales comparison, the adjustment is:
choices: Add $20,000 to the subject's price and ignore the comp
questions.explanation: Adjust the comparable, not the subject. The comp is better, so its price is adjusted downward to match the subject.

questions.stem: Functional obsolescence is a loss in value from:
choices: Outdated design or features, such as a poor floor plan
The land's location next to a park
A nearby factory that is outside the property
Ordinary wear such as a worn roof only
questions.explanation: Physical deterioration is wear and tear. Functional obsolescence is inside the design. External or economic obsolescence comes from outside the property lines.

questions.stem: A house next to a newly announced all-night freight yard loses value. That loss is:
choices: Functional obsolescence from a small closet
questions.explanation: External obsolescence is caused by factors outside the property. It is often incurable by the owner.

questions.stem: Market value is best described as:
choices: The most probable price a willing buyer and willing seller would agree on, neither under unusual pressure, with typical knowledge
The assessed value used for taxes
questions.explanation: Market value assumes an arm's-length deal. Assessed value, list price, and loan amount can differ from it.

questions.stem: The principle that a buyer will not pay more for a property than for an equally desirable substitute is:
questions.explanation: Substitution supports the sales-comparison approach. Contribution asks what one component adds. Anticipation looks at future benefits. Plottage is value created by assembling parcels.

questions.stem: Combining two small lots into one more valuable parcel illustrates:
questions.explanation: Plottage is the increase from assemblage. The act of joining the lots is assemblage. The value bump is plottage.

questions.stem: A swimming pool that costs $40,000 to install but adds only $10,000 in market value illustrates:
questions.explanation: Contribution says an improvement is worth what it adds to value, which may be less than its cost.

questions.stem: Over-improving a house far beyond the neighborhood can run into:
choices: Progression, which would pull it up
questions.explanation: Regression says a high-end property among modest ones tends to be pulled down. Progression is the opposite: a modest home near better ones can be pulled up.

questions.stem: An appraisal is required for many federally related loans because:
choices: The salesperson's listing price is defined as market value by federal law
The buyer prefers not to know the value
The lender needs an independent value opinion from a qualified appraiser
questions.explanation: Federally related transactions generally need an appraisal by a licensed or certified appraiser. A brokerage price opinion does not replace that appraisal. Dollar thresholds change, so the exam point is the role, not a memorized cutoff.

questions.stem: The first broad steps of an appraisal include defining the problem, gathering data, and then:
choices: Applying the relevant approaches and reconciling them into an opinion
questions.explanation: Appraisers define the assignment, collect data, analyze with one or more approaches, and reconcile to a final opinion. They do not negotiate the sale.

questions.stem: A gross rent multiplier is used by:
choices: Dividing sale price by gross rent
Multiplying the tax rate by the assessment
Dividing net operating income by the cap rate
questions.explanation: GRM = price / gross rent. A value estimate is rent × GRM. It is a rough income tool and does not use the full NOI capitalization formula.

questions.stem: Assessed value is used mainly to:
questions.explanation: Assessors assign assessed value for taxation. It may be a fraction of market value. It is not the appraisal the buyer uses to decide what to offer.

questions.stem: Highest and best use means the use that is:
choices: Always the current use, even if illegal
Whatever the current owner enjoys most
The use with the lowest price
Legally allowed, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive
questions.explanation: Appraisers test highest and best use with those four filters. A dream use that zoning forbids is not the highest and best use.

questions.stem: One discount point equals:
choices: One percent of the sale price
One percent of the loan amount
questions.explanation: Points are prepaid interest or a fee computed on the loan, not on the price. Two points on a $200,000 loan cost $4,000.

questions.stem: Loan-to-value ratio compares the loan with:
choices: The value of the property, often the lower of price or appraisal
questions.explanation: LTV = loan ÷ value. Lenders commonly use the lower of the purchase price and the appraised value so the borrower is not financing above market.

questions.stem: Private mortgage insurance is typically required when:
choices: The house is brand new, regardless of down payment
A conventional loan's loan-to-value is above 80 percent
questions.explanation: PMI protects the lender on many conventional loans with less than 20 percent down. FHA uses a mortgage insurance premium, which is a different product. VA loans use a funding fee rather than monthly PMI.

questions.stem: PITI stands for:
questions.explanation: Housing-payment estimates add principal and interest to monthly taxes and insurance. Some estimates also include mortgage insurance or association dues, but the letters PITI mean those four items.

questions.stem: The promissory note is the borrower's:
choices: Deed transferring title to the lender in every state
questions.explanation: The note is the debt instrument. The mortgage or deed of trust is the security instrument that ties the debt to the property.

questions.stem: A clause that lets the lender call the loan due when the property is sold is:
choices: An escalation clause in a purchase offer
questions.explanation: Alienation or due-on-sale lets the lender demand payment if the borrower transfers the property. Defeasance relates to the lien ending when the debt is paid. Acceleration can also be triggered by default.

questions.stem: An amortized loan's monthly payment is structured so that, over the term:
choices: The loan balance declines as principal is paid
The payment is interest only and the balance never changes
Taxes are paid instead of principal
questions.explanation: In a fully amortizing loan, each payment covers interest and some principal, and the balance reaches zero at the end. An interest-only payment does not reduce principal.

questions.stem: An adjustable-rate mortgage differs from a fixed-rate loan because:
choices: The federal government guarantees every ARM
The rate can change with an index, subject to caps in the note
The rate can never change after the first day
questions.explanation: ARMs start with an initial rate and later adjust based on an index plus a margin, usually with periodic and lifetime caps.

questions.stem: FHA's role in a typical FHA-insured loan is to:
choices: Guarantee the loan the way VA does
Lend the money from a local FHA bank branch in every town
questions.explanation: FHA insurance protects the lender. The money usually comes from an approved lender. VA guarantees part of the loan for eligible veterans. USDA has its own rural programs.

questions.stem: A VA loan is best described as:
choices: A loan a lender makes, which VA may guarantee for an eligible veteran
A grant that never has to be repaid
questions.explanation: VA does not usually lend the purchase money itself. It guarantees a portion of a loan made by a lender to an eligible borrower.

questions.stem: Owner financing in which the seller keeps title until the buyer pays an agreed amount is often called:
choices: A land contract or contract for deed
A quitclaim deed delivered on day one with no balance due
questions.explanation: Under a contract for deed, the buyer takes possession and pays over time, and the seller delivers the deed when the contract is satisfied. The buyer has equitable interest and should still be careful about the seller's existing loans.

questions.stem: A bridge loan is commonly used to:
choices: Carry a buyer for a short time between the sale of one home and the purchase of another
questions.explanation: Bridge, or swing, financing is short-term. It is not a long-term amortizing first mortgage and it is not title insurance.

questions.stem: A reverse mortgage is aimed at:
choices: First-time buyers with no down payment required by law in every case
Older homeowners who borrow against equity and generally do not make monthly principal payments
questions.explanation: Reverse mortgages convert home equity into payments to the borrower. They are a distinct product on the financing outline, with age and occupancy rules set by the program.

questions.stem: RESPA's kickback ban means a licensee must not:
choices: Give or accept a thing of value for referring settlement-service business in a covered loan
Tell a buyer the names of three lenders
Charge a commission the seller agreed to in writing
questions.explanation: Section 8 of RESPA prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees for referrals of settlement services in federally related mortgage loans. Sharing a brochure is not the same as paying for a referral.

source.label: Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act § 8, 12 U.S.C. § 2607

questions.stem: Under the TRID rules, a Loan Estimate is generally due:
choices: Only if the borrower asks in the second month
Within three business days after the lender receives an application
questions.explanation: Regulation Z requires the Loan Estimate within three business days of application, and the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before consummation. Those clocks are a favorite exam point.

questions.stem: The Closing Disclosure must generally be received by the borrower:
choices: Within three days after the first payment
At least three business days before consummation
Any time on the day of closing is always enough
questions.explanation: The three-business-day waiting period gives the borrower time to review the Closing Disclosure. Last-minute changes to certain terms can restart the wait.

questions.stem: ECOA prohibits a lender from discriminating in credit because of:
choices: A recent bankruptcy, if applied consistently
Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or the fact that income comes from public assistance
questions.explanation: ECOA is a credit-opportunity law. A lender may still underwrite risk. It may not deny credit because income is from public assistance, or because of the listed personal characteristics.

questions.stem: A borrower's housing-expense ratio and debt-to-income ratio are used in:
choices: Underwriting, to test whether income can carry the payment and other debts
questions.explanation: Underwriters compare PITI, and PITI plus other debts, with gross income. The exam expects you to know what the ratios measure. Program limits change, so a problem will give you the ratio to use.

questions.stem: Risky features the outline flags include:
choices: A fixed rate with no balloon
questions.explanation: A balloon leaves a large balance due at the end. A prepayment penalty charges the borrower for paying early. Both can surprise a borrower and show up in financing questions.

questions.stem: Truth in Lending's advertising rules require that if an ad states a specific triggering term, such as the payment amount, the ad must also:
choices: Disclose the other required loan terms, not a teaser alone
Promise that the rate can never change
questions.explanation: Regulation Z stops ads from dangling a payment or rate without the related disclosures. The APR is the cost-of-credit measure those rules revolve around.

questions.stem: A home-equity line of credit is:
choices: A revolving credit line secured by the home
The same instrument as a quitclaim deed
questions.explanation: A HELOC lets the owner borrow, repay, and borrow again, up to a limit, with the home as security. It is not purchase-money financing by itself, though it can be used at a purchase.

questions.stem: A construction loan is typically:
choices: Short-term financing that funds a build, often followed by permanent financing
A 30-year fixed loan with no draws
questions.explanation: Construction loans are advanced in draws as work is inspected. Many borrowers then replace them with a permanent, or take-out, loan.

questions.stem: Equal monthly payments of principal and interest, with the interest portion largest at the start, describe:
choices: An interest-only loan for the entire term
A land contract with no payments
questions.explanation: Early payments are mostly interest because the balance is highest then. Later payments retire more principal. The payment amount stays level in a standard fixed amortizing loan.

questions.stem: If a buyer assumes a loan that has a due-on-sale clause, the lender may:
choices: Be forced to accept the buyer with no review
Demand full payment unless the lender agrees to the assumption
Convert the loan to a gift
questions.explanation: A due-on-sale clause is why many loans cannot be assumed just because the parties wish it. The lender can call the loan or approve the new borrower.

questions.stem: A valid contract generally requires:
choices: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, and a legal purpose
An earnest-money check in every case
A witness who is the licensee
questions.explanation: Earnest money is common, but the promise to buy and the promise to sell can be the consideration. Without capacity, mutual assent, consideration, and legality, there is no enforceable contract.

questions.stem: The statute of frauds generally requires contracts for the sale of real estate to be:
choices: Spoken in front of two neighbors
questions.explanation: An oral agreement to sell land is usually unenforceable. There are narrow exceptions, but the exam expects the writing rule.

questions.stem: A contract signed by a person who has been adjudicated incompetent is:
choices: Voidable only by the other party
Valid if the price is fair
questions.explanation: A void contract has no legal effect. A voidable contract, such as one signed by a minor in many cases, can be affirmed or rejected by the protected party.

questions.stem: A contract that was once valid but cannot be enforced in court because the deadline to sue has passed is:
questions.explanation: Unenforceable means a defense, such as the statute of limitations or the statute of frauds, blocks a lawsuit. The parties may still perform.

questions.stem: A promise for a promise is:
questions.explanation: Most purchase agreements are bilateral: each side promises. A unilateral contract is accepted by performance, as when a seller promises to pay a fee if a broker produces a buyer, depending on how the listing is written. An option is a classic unilateral contract.

questions.stem: An option agreement gives the optionee:
choices: The duty to buy on the last day
The right, but not the duty, to buy during the option period
questions.explanation: The optionor is bound to sell if the option is exercised. The optionee does not have to exercise it. Consideration keeps the option open.

questions.stem: A seller accepts an offer but changes the closing date. That response is:
choices: A counteroffer, which rejects the original offer
A novation that keeps the original offer alive
questions.explanation: The mirror-image rule means a changed acceptance is a counteroffer. The first offer is dead unless the original offeror accepts the counter.

questions.stem: Two offers arrive the same afternoon. The listing side should:
choices: Present only the offer that pays the larger commission
Wait a week to see who calls again
Present them as the agency agreement and the law require, without burying one
Accept both so both buyers are under contract for the same house
questions.explanation: Multiple offers are presented, not shopped for the licensee's convenience. Only one can be accepted for a full sale unless the parties structure backups. The seller decides.

questions.stem: A financing contingency lets the buyer:
choices: End the contract if the stated financing cannot be obtained, within the contingency's terms
Force the seller to lend the money
questions.explanation: Contingencies are conditions. If a good-faith effort fails, the buyer can usually terminate and recover the deposit as the contract provides. Ignoring the deadline can waive the protection.

questions.stem: 'Time is of the essence' means:
choices: The broker may keep the deposit automatically
The dates in the contract are essential, and missing one can be a breach
The contract need not be in writing
questions.explanation: Without that clause, a short delay is sometimes still substantial performance. With it, the deadline itself matters. Say so in the contract if the parties mean it.

questions.stem: If a buyer breaches and the contract allows the seller to keep the deposit as the sole remedy, that deposit is treated as:
choices: Punitive damages a court must always add on top
A security deposit under landlord-tenant law
questions.explanation: Liquidated damages are an amount agreed in advance. They are different from suing for actual damages or asking a court for specific performance.

questions.stem: Specific performance is a remedy that:
choices: Cancels the contract and returns everyone to the start with no further order
Asks the court to make the parties complete the sale
questions.explanation: Land is treated as unique, so buyers often seek specific performance rather than money alone. Rescission unwinds the deal.

questions.stem: Rescission means the parties:
choices: Must close on a new date only
Are returned, as far as possible, to their positions before the contract
Assign the contract to a lender
questions.explanation: Rescission undoes the contract. Cancellation can end future duties. They are easy to mix up, so read the question for 'back to the start.'

questions.stem: An executory contract is one that:
choices: Has been fully performed by both sides
Has been signed but not yet fully performed
questions.explanation: Executed, in contract language, means fully performed. Executory means duties remain, which is the usual state of a purchase agreement before closing.

questions.stem: Assignment of a contract transfers:
choices: The assignor's rights, and sometimes duties, to another person
questions.explanation: Most contracts can be assigned unless they say otherwise or the duty is personal. Novation substitutes a new contract and releases the original party. Assignment alone may leave the assignor liable.

questions.stem: Novation is:
choices: A new contract that replaces an old one and releases a party
questions.explanation: Use novation when a new buyer takes over and the seller releases the first buyer. A simple assignment may not release the first buyer.

questions.stem: Electronic signatures on a real-estate contract are:
choices: Generally valid when the parties agree to transact electronically and the law's consumer protections are met
Valid only if also carved into stone
questions.explanation: Federal and state electronic-transaction laws give electronic signatures effect. Parties should still keep a record. A signature method does not fix a missing contract term.

questions.stem: Consideration in a purchase agreement can be:
choices: The mutual promises of buyer and seller
questions.explanation: Each side's promise is consideration. Earnest money shows good faith and provides damages or a deposit, but a contract can exist without it.

questions.stem: A minor signs a contract to buy land. In many cases that contract is:
choices: Void against the adult only, with the minor bound
questions.explanation: Minors lack full capacity, so they can usually disaffirm. The adult party generally cannot use the minor's age as the adult's own escape hatch.

questions.stem: Duress or fraud in the inducement typically makes a contract:
questions.explanation: The injured party may affirm or avoid the contract. Fraud as to the nature of the document can sometimes make it void. Either way, it is not a healthy contract.

questions.stem: An offer may be terminated by:
choices: Revocation by the offeror before acceptance, rejection, counteroffer, expiration, or death of a party
Only after the deed is recorded
questions.explanation: Until acceptance, the offeror can usually withdraw. A counteroffer kills the original offer. Deadlines should be in the offer so it does not linger.

questions.stem: Acceptance of an offer is effective, under the mailbox rule often taught for exams, when:
choices: It is properly sent, unless the contract requires actual receipt
questions.explanation: Many exam items treat a properly dispatched acceptance as effective on dispatch. Modern contracts often say acceptance must be received by a deadline. Read the form.

questions.stem: A backup offer should be:
choices: Used to raise the first buyer's price without disclosure
Accepted in full while the first contract is still alive, for the same house
Written so it becomes primary only if the first contract ends, as its terms state
questions.explanation: Two primary contracts for one house are a problem. A backup is expressly secondary. Price shopping a current buyer can also breach agency and contract duties.

questions.stem: If the property is destroyed before closing and the contract is silent, the risk question is serious because:
choices: The parties need the contract's risk-of-loss clause, and equitable title rules may place risk on the buyer in some states
The licensee must rebuild the house
Destruction never affects a real-estate contract
questions.explanation: Risk of loss is a contract and state-law issue. Good forms say who bears a fire before closing and whether insurance proceeds follow the property. Do not guess it away in a client meeting.

questions.stem: A rider that adds an inspection clause to a preprinted offer is:
choices: An addendum or contingency that becomes part of the contract when the parties accept it
questions.explanation: Addenda add terms. Amendments change a contract that already exists. Both should be in writing and signed.

questions.stem: The parties sign an amendment extending the closing date. The document that controls the date is:
choices: The original date, because amendments are informal
questions.explanation: A signed amendment changes the contract. The latest signed writing on that term wins over the earlier page.

questions.stem: Breach occurs when a party:
choices: Asks a question at the inspection
Fails to perform a duty the contract requires, without a legal excuse
questions.explanation: Missing a time-is-of-the-essence deadline, refusing to close, or failing to apply for the loan in good faith can all be breaches, depending on the clause.

questions.stem: A contract with an illegal purpose, such as a sale that requires a discriminatory refusal, is:
choices: Enforceable if the price is high
Voidable only by the discriminating party
questions.explanation: Courts will not enforce an illegal bargain. Fair-housing violations are not a 'term' a contract can legalize.

questions.stem: Earnest money disputes, when the contract names an escrow holder, are resolved by:
choices: The contract's instructions and, if the parties disagree, a process such as interpleader or the written release both sides sign
questions.explanation: The holder is a stakeholder. Paying the wrong person is conversion. The form should say what happens if the deal dies.

questions.stem: Which document actually transfers title at closing in a typical sale?
questions.explanation: The purchase agreement is a contract to convey. Title passes when a valid deed is delivered and accepted, subject to recording for priority against later buyers.

questions.stem: A purchase agreement is executory until:
choices: The parties have performed, usually by delivering the deed and paying the price
questions.explanation: Signing starts the executory period. Closing is the usual moment the sale contract is executed in the sense of fully performed.

questions.stem: Competency of parties looks at whether a person:
choices: Understands the nature of the act and is of legal age, or has a valid representative
Lives in the same town as the property
questions.explanation: Age and mental capacity matter. A conservator or attorney-in-fact may sign if that person has authority. The licensee should not coach an impaired seller through a signature.

questions.stem: A unilateral contract is formed when:
choices: A promise is exchanged for a promise
A deed is recorded in every case
questions.explanation: Silence is not acceptance. In a unilateral setup, doing the act accepts the offer. Bilateral contracts are promise for promise.

questions.stem: If a contingency deadline passes and the buyer does nothing, the usual risk is that:
choices: The contract becomes void with no further duty
The seller must cut the price
The contingency is waived and the buyer must proceed
questions.explanation: Many forms say the contingency dies, and the contract continues, unless the buyer objects in time. Read the clause. Some forms auto-terminate. The point is that deadlines are not decorative.

questions.stem: Mutual mistake about the identity of the parcel can make a contract:
choices: Voidable, because there was no real agreement on the subject
A warranty that the wrong lot is fine
questions.explanation: If both parties think they are bargaining for different things, assent failed. A court can rescind. A small mistake about value is not the same as a mistake about which lot.

questions.stem: The licensee's job with a preprinted form is to:
choices: Leave the price blank and fill it in after closing
Fill in factual blanks the parties agree to, and send legal questions to a lawyer
Invent clauses that rewrite state law
Tell the client the form is a substitute for advice in a dispute
questions.explanation: Licensees are not lawyers. Completing a standard form as the parties direct is normal. Drafting custom legal language, or giving legal advice, is the unauthorized practice of law.

questions.stem: A client is the person to whom the licensee owes fiduciary duties. A customer is:
choices: Always the person who pays the commission
A person the licensee works with but does not represent
questions.explanation: Payment does not by itself decide who is the client. The representation agreement does. Customers are owed honesty and fairness, not loyalty.

questions.stem: The fiduciary duties often remembered as obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care are owed to:
choices: Every customer in the same degree as the client
questions.explanation: Those duties run to the principal. Honesty and disclosure of material facts still run to customers and other parties. Loyalty does not mean helping the other side against the client.

questions.stem: Loyalty means the licensee must:
choices: Share the client's bottom line with the other side to be friendly
Buy the property without telling the client
Hide material defects if the client asks
Put the client's interests ahead of the licensee's own
questions.explanation: Self-dealing and secret profits breach loyalty. Loyalty never excuses fraud or concealment of material facts.

questions.stem: A licensee who wants to buy the client's listing must:
choices: Wait until after recording and then reveal the purchase
Disclose that interest and avoid using the client's confidential information against the client
Stay silent so the price stays low
Assign the listing to a friend with no disclosure
questions.explanation: Buying from a client is a conflict. Disclosure and informed consent, in writing, are the safe path. The client should understand the licensee is no longer only an advocate.

questions.stem: Confidentiality requires the licensee to keep secret:
choices: Facts already in a public recorded plat
The client's bargaining position, motivation, and other confidential information
Information the law requires to be disclosed
questions.explanation: Confidential information stays confidential even after the relationship ends. Material property defects are not confidential. They must be disclosed.

questions.stem: Accounting, as a fiduciary duty, means:
choices: The licensee may pool deposits with personal funds if the math is accurate
The client must do the broker's taxes
The licensee must track and report money and property held for the client
questions.explanation: Every dollar of other people's money is accounted for. Commingling and conversion are the failures of this duty.

questions.stem: Obedience means the licensee follows lawful instructions. It does not mean:
choices: Following an instruction to hide a material defect or to discriminate
Using the price the client set
Following a lawful instruction on showing times
Presenting an offer the client asked to see
questions.explanation: Illegal or unethical instructions are refused. The rest of the client's lawful directions are followed.

questions.stem: An agency relationship can be created by:
choices: A written agreement, and in some cases by conduct that leads a person to believe they are represented
The deed at the end of the deal only
A newspaper ad with no more contact
questions.explanation: Express agency is the written agreement the state usually requires before negotiating. Implied agency can still arise from conduct, which is a reason to be clear about who is represented.

questions.stem: A special agent is authorized to:
choices: Bind the client on any subject forever
Handle one specific transaction or task
questions.explanation: A real-estate broker is usually a special agent. A general agent handles a range of matters, as a property manager might. A universal agent may do nearly everything, usually under a broad power of attorney.

questions.stem: A property manager hired to run a building on an ongoing basis is closest to:
choices: A universal agent with no limits
A transaction broker in every state
questions.explanation: Ongoing management authority is broader than a single sale. It is still not unlimited. The management agreement sets the bounds.

questions.stem: A transaction broker, or facilitator, where that status exists, is:
choices: A licensee who assists without being the fiduciary agent of either side
questions.explanation: Non-agency roles still require honesty and care with the paperwork. They are not a free pass to favor one side in secret. Some states do not use this status.

questions.stem: Dual agency means:
choices: Two different companies each represent their own client
The same brokerage or licensee represents both parties in the same transaction
questions.explanation: Dual agency is lawful only with informed consent where the state allows it. The licensee cannot fully advocate for both sides at once, which is why consent and limits on confidential information matter.

questions.stem: A designated-agency arrangement tries to:
choices: Eliminate the need for any disclosure
Convert the firm into a lender
Appoint different licensees in one firm to advocate for each party
questions.explanation: Designated agency, where allowed, lets each side have an advocate inside one firm. The firm and the people who supervise both sides may still have dual-agency limits.

questions.stem: An exclusive-right-to-sell listing means the broker earns a commission if:
choices: Only the listing broker personally finds the buyer
The property is withdrawn and never sold
A neighbor mentions the house and nothing more happens
The property sells during the listing term, no matter who procures the buyer
questions.explanation: Exclusive agency lets the owner sell without a commission if the owner finds the buyer alone. Open listings pay only the broker who procures. Exclusive right to sell is the broadest.

questions.stem: An open listing pays:
choices: Every broker who ever showed the house, in full
Only the broker who procures a ready, willing, and able buyer, and the owner may list with several brokers
questions.explanation: Open listings are nonexclusive. The procuring cause earns the fee. They are less common than exclusive listings and can create procuring-cause fights.

questions.stem: A buyer-representation agreement should state:
choices: The duties, the compensation, the term, and how the broker may be paid
That the buyer owes no duty to tell the truth
questions.explanation: Buyer agreements create the agency, say when it ends, and explain compensation, including whether the buyer pays if the seller does not offer it.

questions.stem: Agency ends when:
choices: The purpose is completed, the term expires, the parties agree, or the law ends it, such as by death of the client or destruction of the property
questions.explanation: Completion and expiration are the clean endings. Death, incapacity, destruction, or bankruptcy can end it by law. Some duties, especially confidentiality and accounting, survive.

questions.stem: A power of attorney used to sign a deed should be:
choices: Assumed because the person is a relative
A substitute for the buyer's loan approval
A written authority that actually covers that act, from a competent principal
A verbal request at the closing table
questions.explanation: The agent under a power of attorney is an attorney-in-fact. The document must authorize the sale. Licensees do not invent authority that is not written.

questions.stem: Commingling is:
choices: Keeping a copy of the contract
Mixing client funds with the licensee's own money
Splitting a commission with the cooperating broker
Depositing earnest money in the broker's trust account
questions.explanation: Trust money stays in the trust account. Mixing it with operating or personal funds is commingling. Spending it is conversion, which is worse.

questions.stem: Conversion is:
choices: Changing a list price with the seller's written consent
Moving a deposit from the salesperson to the broker's trust account
Using trust money as if it belonged to the licensee
questions.explanation: Conversion is theft of funds held for others. It is among the fastest ways to lose a license and face criminal charges.

questions.stem: A licensee owes a customer:
choices: Confidential treatment of the customer's bottom line if the licensee represents the other side
Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of material facts
A duty to follow the customer's illegal instructions
questions.explanation: Customers are not clients. You still may not lie to them or hide defects. You also may not give them your client's secrets.

questions.stem: The procuring cause of a sale is the broker who:
choices: Printed the most flyers, even if another broker wrote the accepted offer
Started an uninterrupted chain of events that led to the agreement
questions.explanation: Procuring cause is about who produced the buyer, not who spent the most on ads. Open-listing and commission disputes turn on it.

questions.stem: A net listing is risky because:
choices: The broker's interest in a higher price can conflict with the client's interest, and some states bar the form
It removes all duty to disclose defects
It always produces the best price for the seller
It is required by federal law
questions.explanation: If the broker keeps everything above a net figure, the temptation is to hide the true value. Many states prohibit net listings. Connecticut's regulation does.

questions.stem: Reasonable care means the licensee:
choices: Skips questions that might slow a sale
Uses the skill a competent licensee would use, including checking facts the licensee can check
Guarantees the house will rise in value
questions.explanation: Care includes accurate information, timely presentation of offers, and knowing when a question belongs to a lawyer, inspector, or appraiser.

questions.stem: Disclosure of material facts to a customer is required even when:
choices: The fact is the licensee's home address
The fact is the client's confidential divorce timing and nothing about the property
The client asks the licensee to stay quiet
The fact is a rumor with no basis
questions.explanation: Client instructions stop at the law. A known material defect is disclosed. A client's personal motivation usually is not.

questions.stem: Subagency, in the older multiple-listing model, meant:
choices: A broker who represented only the buyer
A cooperating broker who represented the seller, not the buyer
questions.explanation: Before buyer agency was common, cooperating brokers were often subagents of the seller. Treating a buyer as a client while legally working for the seller was a frequent source of undisclosed dual agency.

questions.stem: An agency disclosure should be made:
choices: Early, before confidential information is exchanged, as state law requires
In the advertisement's fine print a year later
questions.explanation: The point of early disclosure is that people should know whom you represent before they tell you their secrets. Connecticut requires this by the first personal meeting.

questions.stem: A licensee who represents the seller and also helps the buyer 'just a little' with offer strategy, without consent, risks:
questions.explanation: Advice that looks like advocacy can create an implied agency. If you already represent the seller, that implied duty to the buyer is an undisclosed dual agency.

questions.stem: A material fact is a fact that:
choices: The licensee would rather not discuss
A reasonable buyer would consider important in deciding whether to buy, or at what price
The seller finds embarrassing but that does not affect the property
questions.explanation: Material facts affect the decision. A cracked foundation is material. A seller's dislike of the paint color may not be.

questions.stem: Latent defects are:
choices: Open permits posted on the door
Defects the seller painted over that everyone can see from the sidewalk
Hidden problems a buyer might not see in an ordinary look
questions.explanation: Latent means hidden. Known latent defects are exactly the facts licensees get in trouble for concealing. Patent defects are obvious.

questions.stem: A licensee who knows the basement floods and says 'dry as a bone' has:
questions.explanation: Puffing is vague opinion, such as 'charming street.' A false statement about flooding is fraud or misrepresentation, not sales talk.

questions.stem: Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to most housing built before:
choices: 1960 only if the buyer has a child
questions.explanation: Congress chose 1978, when residential lead paint was banned. Sellers and landlords of most pre-1978 housing must disclose known lead information and give the required pamphlet.

source.label: Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act, 42 U.S.C. § 4852d

questions.stem: Under the federal lead law, a buyer of pre-1978 housing must be given:
choices: A 10-day period to conduct a lead inspection or risk assessment, unless the parties agree otherwise
Nothing, if the licensee is in a hurry
A deed that guarantees no lead is present
A waiver the seller can sign alone
questions.explanation: The statute gives the purchaser 10 days, unless they mutually agree on a different period. The buyer may waive the inspection, but the waiver has to be the buyer's.

source.label: Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act, 42 U.S.C. § 4852d

questions.stem: Which environmental issue is a classic disclosure and inspection topic?
questions.explanation: Tanks, radon, asbestos, lead, mold, and contaminated soil can affect health and value. They belong in the disclosure conversation, not in small talk only.

questions.stem: A seller's property condition form is best understood as:
choices: The seller's statement of known condition, not a warranty and not a substitute for inspection
A guarantee the house is perfect
questions.explanation: Condition forms pass on knowledge. They do not replace an inspector, and they do not usually create a new warranty. Buyers who waive inspections take on more risk.

questions.stem: If a licensee sees a stain, a sagging beam, or a strong mildew smell, the careful step is to:
choices: Disclose the red flag and suggest the buyer have it inspected
Say nothing unless the seller agrees
Paint over it before the open house
questions.explanation: You do not have to be the engineer. You do have to pass on what you actually see and not talk a buyer out of a reasonable inspection.

questions.stem: Stigmatized-property rules differ by state. A safe national approach is:
choices: Disclose physical and legal conditions the law treats as material, and follow the state's rule on deaths or reputational facts
Always advertise every death in the headline
Ask the neighbors to gossip on camera
questions.explanation: Physical defects travel with you in every state. Whether a death or a felony must be volunteered is state-specific. Connecticut defines some of those facts as nonmaterial unless the buyer asks in writing.

questions.stem: Fair housing advertising should describe:
choices: The property, not the kind of people the seller hopes will live there
That families with children are unwelcome in an ordinary rental
questions.explanation: Describe the house, the price, and the features. Words that state a preference about a protected class are illegal advertising, with narrow exceptions such as housing for older persons that actually qualifies.

questions.stem: A proposed use that would need a zoning change should be:
choices: Identified before the buyer is bound, so the contract can address the approval
Treated as a title defect only
questions.explanation: Use and zoning are disclosure and contract issues. A contingency for permits keeps the buyer from being forced to buy a property that cannot be used as planned.

questions.stem: Radon is:
choices: A colorless gas that can enter buildings from the soil and is commonly tested in home inspections
questions.explanation: Radon is an environmental disclosure topic. Testing is routine in many markets. The licensee does not invent a reading; the licensee does not hide a known test.

questions.stem: Asbestos is most concerning when:
choices: It is known and left undisturbed, and someone pretends that means it was never present
It is used as a financing term
It is friable or will be disturbed by renovation
It is a type of easement
questions.explanation: Intact, undisturbed asbestos is often managed in place. Sanding or demolition can release fibers. Known asbestos is a disclosure item, not a decorating tip.

questions.stem: A seller says a prior owner removed an underground tank but has no closure letter. The licensee should:
choices: State in the ad that the tank was certified removed
Fill the hole and move on
Forget it because the yard looks mowed
Treat the incomplete history as a fact to disclose and a reason for the buyer to investigate
questions.explanation: You report what is known, including the gaps. Inventing a clean closure is misrepresentation.

questions.stem: Government disclosure requirements on the national outline include:
choices: A duty to guarantee future value
A duty to advertise the seller's medical chart
Lead-based paint disclosure for most pre-1978 housing
A duty to hide flood maps
questions.explanation: Lead disclosure is the federal item the outline names. Flood zones, coastal rules, and local forms may add more. When a map or a seller's knowledge shows a hazard, do not bury it.

questions.stem: Puffing is:
choices: Exaggerated opinion that a reasonable person would not treat as a hard fact
A false statement about the roof's age
questions.explanation: 'Best view in town' is puffing if nobody would take it as a measurement. 'New roof in 2024' is a fact, and it must be true.

questions.stem: A buyer asks whether the roof leaks. The licensee knows it does. The honest answer is:
choices: Yes, and the buyer should inspect it
A promise to pay for a new roof
'Not that I know of,' to protect the seller
Silence, then a change of subject
questions.explanation: Direct questions about known defects get direct answers. Dodging is concealment.

questions.stem: Surveys are warranted when:
choices: Boundaries, encroachments, or the legal description are in doubt
The buyer wants to skip closing
The house is a condominium with no land interest of any kind and no question has been raised
The licensee already guessed the lot lines
questions.explanation: A survey locates improvements and boundaries on the ground. It is the tool for encroachments and for checking that the fence is actually on the lot. The outline ties surveys to property condition and land use.

questions.stem: A property manager's basic client is:
choices: The tenant, in the same fiduciary way
questions.explanation: The management agreement creates an agency with the owner. Tenants are owed honest dealing and compliance with housing law, not the owner's loyalty.

questions.stem: A gross lease typically means the tenant pays:
choices: Rent plus taxes, insurance, and maintenance
A percentage of gross sales only, with no base rent ever
A fixed rent, and the landlord pays the operating expenses
questions.explanation: Gross: landlord carries the operating costs. Net: tenant pays some or all of them. Percentage: rent is tied to sales, often with a base rent.

questions.stem: A triple-net lease commonly shifts to the tenant:
choices: The purchase price of the building
questions.explanation: Net, double-net, and triple-net describe how many expense categories the tenant picks up. The exam's plain meaning of triple-net is taxes, insurance, and maintenance.

questions.stem: A percentage lease is most often used for:
choices: Retail space, with rent tied in part to the tenant's sales
A week-to-week room in a house only
questions.explanation: Retail landlords use percentage rent so the rent reflects the store's success. There is often a base rent plus a percentage above a breakpoint.

questions.stem: An estate for years is a lease:
choices: That the tenant may hold after eviction without paying
For a definite period, with a start and an end
That renews forever unless a court ends it
questions.explanation: The name is old. The term can be months or years, as long as the end date is certain. No notice is required to end it on that date unless the lease says otherwise.

questions.stem: A month-to-month tenancy is:
choices: An estate for years with a fixed end date five years out
A periodic tenancy that renews each month until proper notice is given
questions.explanation: Periodic tenancies roll on until notice. Tenancy at sufferance is a holdover without permission. Tenancy at will is open-ended and ends at either party's will, as state law allows.

questions.stem: A tenant who stays after the lease ends, without the landlord's consent, holds:
choices: A joint tenancy with the landlord
questions.explanation: The landlord may accept rent and create a new periodic tenancy, or treat the occupant as a holdover and pursue possession. The occupant is not a guest and not a fee owner.

questions.stem: Security deposits in a management account should be:
choices: Kept separate from the manager's operating money and handled as trust funds
Returned to the owner as a fee on day one
Converted to cash and stored in a desk
Spent on office rent as long as the manager remembers the amount
questions.explanation: Other people's money is trust money. State law sets the maximum deposit, the account, interest, and the return deadline. Connecticut's statute is specific.

questions.stem: Fair housing in property management means the manager must not:
choices: Screen for ability to pay the rent
Refuse a qualified applicant because of a protected class, or apply rules unevenly
Enforce a reasonable occupancy limit based on local codes
questions.explanation: Screening for income, credit, and rental history is lawful when it is consistent. Screening for race, familial status, disability, or another protected class is not. Reasonable accommodations are part of the job.

questions.stem: The Americans with Disabilities Act, in a property-management setting, is most directly about:
choices: Access to public areas and reasonable changes for people with disabilities
questions.explanation: Title III covers public accommodations. A rental office open to the public is in that world. Residential units also face fair-housing modification and accommodation rules, which are a related but separate statute.

source.label: Americans with Disabilities Act, title III

questions.stem: Setting rent is primarily a function of:
choices: A number that excludes all vacant units nearby
Market comparison: what similar units actually rent for
questions.explanation: A rent schedule looks at competing units, vacancy, condition, and concessions. Charging whatever the owner hopes for, with no market check, produces empty units.

questions.stem: A ground lease is a lease of:
choices: Only the top floor of a tower for a weekend
Land, often long-term, on which the tenant may build
questions.explanation: Ground leases separate ownership of the land from the building the tenant constructs. They are long, and the improvement may revert to the landowner at the end.

questions.stem: Title passes from seller to buyer when:
choices: A valid deed is delivered and accepted
questions.explanation: Delivery and acceptance of the deed transfer title. Recording protects that title against later claimants. It is not what makes the deed effective between the parties.

questions.stem: A general warranty deed promises that the grantor will:
choices: Transfer only whatever interest the grantor has, with no promises
Defend the title against claims arising both before and during the grantor's ownership
Guarantee the property's future market value
questions.explanation: General warranty gives the broadest title covenants. Special warranty usually covers only the grantor's own period of ownership. A quitclaim makes no title promises.

questions.stem: A quitclaim deed:
choices: Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties
questions.explanation: Quitclaim deeds are used to clear clouds, release claims, or transfer between people who know each other. They are a weak deed for an arm's-length buyer who wants promises.

questions.stem: Recording a deed gives:
choices: A guarantee that the grantor owned the land
questions.explanation: Constructive notice means later buyers are treated as if they knew what is in the land records. Recording does not cure a forged deed or a deed from someone who never owned the land.

questions.stem: A chain of title is:
choices: The history of conveyances linking the present owner back to earlier owners
questions.explanation: Title searches follow the chain. A break, a missing spouse's signature, or an unreleased lien is a cloud.

questions.stem: Marketable title is title a reasonable buyer would accept because it is:
choices: Free of undisclosed defects that would expose the buyer to litigation or doubt
Perfect in a philosophical sense and free of zoning
Whatever the seller says it is
Insured, even if a known defect remains
questions.explanation: Marketable does not mean there is no easement for a utility. It means there is no serious, unresolved defect. Insurable title is different: a title company may insure over a problem the buyer could still object to as unmarketable.

questions.stem: Title insurance protects the insured against:
choices: Covered title defects that exist at the policy date and were not excluded
questions.explanation: The policy is about title as of the date, subject to exceptions. It is not a home warranty and not hazard insurance.

questions.stem: An owner's title policy is usually paid for at closing and protects:
choices: The owner, for as long as that owner or the owner's heirs have an interest
Only the lender, and only until the first payment
questions.explanation: The lender's policy protects the mortgagee and shrinks as the loan is paid. The owner's policy protects the buyer. Who pays is a contract term, but the roles are different.

questions.stem: A cloud on title is:
choices: A rain delay at the open house
A claim, lien, or break that makes ownership uncertain
questions.explanation: Clouds are removed by releases, corrective deeds, or a quiet-title action. Ignoring a cloud is how closings get postponed.

questions.stem: Prorations at closing divide:
choices: Items such as taxes, rent, and association dues so each side pays its share of the period
The commission according to federal law
Personal property that was excluded from the sale
questions.explanation: The closing statement shows credits and debits. The contract should say whether the seller or the buyer owns the day of closing, and whether the year is 360 or 365 days.

questions.stem: A short sale is a sale in which:
choices: The buyer pays cash in under an hour
The listing period is under one week
The lender agrees to accept less than the full mortgage balance
questions.explanation: The lender is a necessary participant because the sale will not retire the whole debt. Short sales take lender approval and can fail late.

questions.stem: Foreclosure is:
choices: The legal process a lender uses to enforce a lien after default
A voluntary gift of the deed with no default
questions.explanation: Judicial foreclosure goes through court. Nonjudicial foreclosure follows a power-of-sale clause where state law allows it. Either way, the lien is being enforced.

questions.stem: A home warranty is:
choices: The same as an owner's title policy
A service contract covering certain repairs for a stated term
questions.explanation: Warranties, title insurance, and homeowners insurance solve different problems. The exam expects you to keep them apart.

questions.stem: Essential elements of a valid deed include:
choices: Consideration that must be the full market value and nothing less
A competent grantor, a grantee, words of conveyance, a description, and delivery
questions.explanation: Deeds can recite nominal consideration. They still need a granting clause, an identifiable property, and delivery. Recording is strongly wise and often essential for priority, but delivery is what moves title between the parties.

questions.stem: A special warranty deed limits the grantor's defense of title to:
choices: Defects that arose during the grantor's ownership
No defects at all, like a quitclaim
Every defect back to the sovereign
questions.explanation: Special, or limited, warranty is narrower than general warranty and broader than quitclaim. Foreclosure and fiduciary deeds are often limited.

questions.stem: Escrow at closing is used so that:
choices: The deed can be signed in pencil and never delivered
A neutral holder can follow the parties' instructions and disburse when conditions are met
The salesperson can spend the deposit
questions.explanation: The escrow holder is a stakeholder. Conditions such as loan funding, title, and prorations are satisfied before money and the deed trade places.

questions.stem: A corrective deed is used to:
choices: Fix an error in an earlier deed, such as a misspelled name or a bad description
questions.explanation: Corrections should be documented, not whispered. A new deed that says it corrects the earlier one, properly executed and recorded, is the usual cure.

questions.stem: Probate sales differ because:
choices: The personal representative's authority and the court's oversight can limit how the sale is made
The property is always exempt from disclosure rules that otherwise apply
The buyer cannot obtain title insurance
questions.explanation: The outline flags probate as a special process. The seller is acting in a fiduciary role. Deadlines, notices, and court confirmation may apply. Ask who has authority to sign.

questions.stem: The federal Fair Housing Act's named protected classes include:
choices: Age and marital status, which are the federal list
Credit score, occupation, and hairstyle only
Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability
questions.explanation: Those seven are the statute's classes. Age and marital status are not federal fair-housing classes, though a state like Connecticut adds them. Familial status protects households with children under 18.

questions.stem: Blockbusting is:
choices: Persuading owners to sell by playing on fear that a protected class is moving in
Refusing a loan because of the neighborhood's racial makeup
Directing buyers only toward certain neighborhoods
questions.explanation: Blockbusting is the panic-selling tactic. Redlining is discriminatory lending or insurance by area. Steering is directing people toward or away from neighborhoods because of a protected class.

questions.stem: Steering is:
choices: Adjusting a comparable sale for a garage
A lawful request for a first-floor unit by a person who needs it
Guiding buyers or renters toward or away from areas because of a protected class
questions.explanation: Choices belong to the customer. Suggestions based on race, religion, or familial status are steering. Answering a request for features, such as one-floor living, is not.

questions.stem: Redlining is:
choices: Refusing to lend or insure based on the racial or ethnic character of a neighborhood
Drawing a boundary on a survey
questions.explanation: The name comes from lines once drawn on maps. It is illegal whether or not anyone still uses a red pen.

questions.stem: A housing provider must allow a person with a disability to make reasonable modifications to the unit, typically:
choices: Only after a variance from the real-estate commission
Never, if the landlord prefers matching paint
At the tenant's expense, when needed for full enjoyment, with restoration rules the statute allows
Only if the modification is free to everyone else as well
questions.explanation: Fair housing requires reasonable modifications and reasonable accommodations. A landlord may, when it is reasonable, condition a rental modification on restoring the interior, fair wear excepted.

questions.stem: Which statement may violate fair-housing advertising rules?
choices: 'Perfect for a single professional, no kids'
questions.explanation: Describe the property. 'No kids' discriminates based on familial status unless the housing qualifies as housing for older persons. Marital and family preferences are a common trap.

questions.stem: An antitrust violation in real estate is:
choices: A seller negotiating a lower fee
Brokers agreeing to charge the same commission
Two brokers cooperating on one sale with their clients' consent
One broker independently choosing a fee
questions.explanation: Price fixing is a Sherman Act problem. Each brokerage sets its own fees. A seller may always try to negotiate. Cooperation on a listing is not the same as a conspiracy to fix prices.

questions.stem: Dividing a town so each brokerage agrees to stay out of the others' areas is:
questions.explanation: Allocating territories or customers is a restraint of trade. So is a group boycott of a discount broker.

questions.stem: The National Do Not Call rules mean a licensee should:
choices: Call anyone, because real estate is exempt from the registry entirely
Not call numbers on the registry to solicit, unless an exception such as an existing business relationship applies
questions.explanation: The Telemarketing Sales Rule applies to sales calls. An established business relationship is a limited exception, often up to 18 months after a transaction or 3 months after an inquiry. Company-specific do-not-call requests still control.

questions.stem: A salesperson's online ad should:
choices: Identify the licensee and the brokerage in the way state rules require, and stay accurate
Look like a private owner if that gets more clicks
Promise that every listed home will appreciate
Hide the brokerage because the page is personal
questions.explanation: Technology does not repeal advertising rules. The firm name, a current price, and no false urgency are the baseline. Connecticut's regulation is specific about names and contact information.

questions.stem: Commingling client funds is:
choices: Required, so the broker earns interest
A violation of the duty to account and a common ground for discipline
The same as issuing a receipt
questions.explanation: Trust money is separated, documented, and disbursed only as instructions allow. A receipt is good. Mixing the money is not.

questions.stem: An independent-contractor salesperson usually:
choices: Is paid only an hourly wage with taxes withheld in every state by statute
Has no broker and needs no license
Cannot be held to advertising rules
Controls work hours and is paid by commission, under a written agreement, while the broker still supervises licensed activity
questions.explanation: The tax status and the licensing status are different. A 1099 worker can still be supervised for license-law purposes. Connecticut even has a statutory liability rule for independent-contractor salespersons.

questions.stem: Due diligence in a transaction means:
choices: Closing as fast as possible with no questions
Taking reasonable steps to verify information and to recommend the right experts
Replacing the attorney, inspector, and appraiser
questions.explanation: Due diligence is investigation. Licensees coordinate it. They do not pretend to be every profession on the closing checklist.
